🟢 PART 1 — Nasal Cavity, Paranasal Sinuses, Nasopharynx & Larynx

🗺️ 1.1 Respiratory System — the big map

  • Upper respiratory tract: nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx
  • Lower respiratory tract: trachea → primary bronchi → lungs
  • Think of it as one continuous tube that air travels down — every structure below is just "one more stop" on that tube.
👆 Click a station to jump straight to it. We'll walk this exact path, lecture-order.

👃 1.2 Nasal Cavity

  • Extent: nostrils (anterior) → posterior nasal apertures / choanae → opens into nasopharynx
  • Division: nasal septum splits it into right & left halves
  • Each half has 4 walls: roof, floor, medial wall (septum), lateral wall

Roof

  • Anterior: nasal + frontal bones (sloping)
  • Middle: cribriform plate of ethmoid — perforated, lets olfactory nerve fibers through
  • Posterior: sloping body of sphenoid + opening of sphenoid sinus

Floor (= hard palate)

  • Palatine process of maxilla
  • Horizontal plate of palatine bone

Medial wall = Nasal septum

  • Vertical, in the median plane
  • Septal cartilage — anterior
  • Perpendicular plate of ethmoid — posterosuperior
  • Vomer — posteroinferior

Lateral wall — conchae & meatuses

🔧 Why 3 shelves?

Each concha (turbinate) is a bony shelf that curls air into a thin, swirling sheet — more surface area → better warming, humidifying and filtering before air reaches the lungs. The space under each concha is its meatus, and that's where things drain in.

  • Superior, middle, inferior conchae → 3 spaces below them = superior/middle/inferior meatus
  • Inferior concha = its own separate skull bone; superior + middle conchae = projections of the ethmoid bone
Spheno-ethmoidal recess (above superior concha): sphenoidal sinus opens here.
Superior meatus: posterior ethmoid sinuses open here.
Middle meatus shows: bulla ethmoidalis (swelling from middle ethmoid cells) and hiatus semilunaris (curved groove below the bulla, leading to the funnel-shaped infundibulum).
Opens here: Frontal sinus, Anterior ethmoid sinus, Maxillary sinus → mnemonic FAM.
Inferior meatus: receives the nasolacrimal duct (that's why your nose runs when you cry!).
✅ Quick check

Which 3 sinuses drain into the middle meatus? → Frontal, Anterior ethmoid, Maxillary (FAM)

🧪 1.3 Mucous membrane regions & their jobs

🔧 Structure matches function

Three zones, three jobs:

  • Vestibule (most anterior): modified skin with coarse hairs → traps large particles at the door
  • Olfactory region (above superior concha): olfactory epithelium with smell-sensing nerve endings
  • Respiratory region (rest of cavity): respiratory mucosa with a huge venous plexus underneath → warms inspired air; surface mucus traps smaller particles/organisms

🩸 1.4 Vessels, nerves & Little's area

Arterial supply

  • From external carotid artery (via maxillary artery): Sphenopalatine artery, Greater palatine artery; + septal branch of superior labial artery (from facial artery)
  • From internal carotid artery (via ophthalmic artery): Anterior & posterior ethmoidal arteries

🚨 Mechanism: Epistaxis (nosebleeds)

Little's area sits on the antero-inferior septum, just above the vestibule — it's where all 4 arteries above meet and anastomose (= Kiesselbach's plexus). Thin mucosa + dense vessel crossover = the single most common bleeding site in the nose.

Anterior ethmoidal artery — branch of ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system). Enters from above/front.
Sphenopalatine artery — branch of maxillary artery (external carotid system). Usually the dominant supply, enters from behind.
Greater palatine artery — branch of maxillary artery, climbs up from below through the incisive canal.
Septal branch of superior labial artery — branch of facial artery (external carotid system), enters from the front/below.
👆 Tap each artery name to recall its origin — all 4 converge right here on the septum.

Venous drainage

  • Anterior → facial vein
  • Posterior → pterygoid & pharyngeal venous plexuses
  • Superior → cavernous sinus ⚠

Nerve supply

  • General sensation: ophthalmic (V1) & maxillary (V2) divisions of trigeminal nerve (CN V)
  • Special sensation (smell): olfactory nerves (CN I) → pass through cribriform plate → olfactory bulb

Lymph drainage

  • Vestibule → submandibular nodes
  • Rest of nasal cavity → upper deep cervical nodes

🫧 1.5 Paranasal Sinuses

  • Air-filled cavities inside maxilla, frontal, sphenoid & ethmoid bones, lined by mucoperiosteum, opening into the nasal cavity
  • Functions: (1) secrete mucus → keeps nasal cavity moist/clean (2) lighten the skull (3) act as resonators for the voice
Within body of sphenoid bone → opens into spheno-ethmoidal recess.
Largest sinus; pyramidal; roof = floor of orbit, floor = roots of upper molar/premolar teeth → opens into middle meatus via hiatus semilunaris. Its drainage hole sits near the roof — against gravity — so it's the sinus that gets infected most often.
Paired, triangular, variable size → opens into middle meatus via the infundibulum (anterior end of hiatus semilunaris).
3 groups — anterior & middle open into middle meatus (anterior via hiatus semilunaris, middle on/above the bulla); posterior opens into superior meatus.

🚨 Applied anatomy — how infection mechanically spreads

  • Sinusitis: maxillary sinus most commonly infected — its drainage orifice is near its roof, so gravity works against drainage
  • Nasal cavity connects to: anterior cranial fossa (via cribriform plate), nasopharynx (→ middle ear via Eustachian tube), and all paranasal sinuses — one continuous mucosal network, so infection can track between all of them
  • Only thin bone separates sphenoidal sinus from the pituitary fossa → surgeons reach the pituitary gland through the nose (transsphenoidal surgery)
  • Little's area = most common epistaxis site (see above)

🔽 1.6 Pharynx & Nasopharynx

  • Pharynx = musculo-membranous tube, shared pathway for food and air
  • Site: behind nasal cavities, mouth & larynx
  • Extent: skull base → lower border of C6 vertebra, then continues as esophagus

Nasopharynx

  • Position: above soft palate, behind nasal cavity
  • Pharyngeal isthmus: gap between soft palate & posterior pharyngeal wall; closed by soft palate during swallowing (stops food refluxing into the nose)
  • Lateral wall: opening of auditory (Eustachian) tube → tubal elevation above/behind it → salpingopharyngeal fold (mucosa over salpingopharyngeus muscle) → pharyngeal recess just behind the tubal elevation
  • Pharyngeal tonsil at the roof — if enlarged in children = adenoids, can block the nasopharynx completely → forces mouth breathing. Normally atrophies after puberty.

Blood / lymph / nerve supply of pharynx

  • Arteries: ascending pharyngeal, lingual, tonsillar branch of facial, branches of maxillary
  • Veins: pharyngeal plexus → internal jugular vein
  • Lymph: retropharyngeal nodes or directly to deep cervical nodes
  • Motor: pharyngeal plexus = pharyngeal branch of vagus (CN X) — except stylopharyngeus, which is supplied by glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
  • Sensory, by region: Nasopharynx → maxillary nerve (CN V2); Oropharynx → glossopharyngeal (CN IX); Laryngopharynx → internal laryngeal branch of vagus (CN X)

🎤 1.7 Larynx — gross anatomy (Tutorial 1)

  • Definition: fibro-musculo-cartilaginous tube in the anterior midline of the neck — voice production + air passage
  • Position: below tongue & hyoid bone, between the great neck vessels
  • Extent: root of tongue → trachea; vertebral level C4–C6
  • Communication: opens above into the laryngeal part of the pharynx (laryngopharynx), continues below as trachea
  • Relations: anterior = infrahyoid muscles; sides = thyroid gland
  • Structure: cartilages (skeleton) + joints/ligaments/membranes + muscles (move cartilages) + mucous membrane (lines cavity)

Cartilages — 3 unpaired + 3 paired

  • Unpaired: Thyroid (largest — 2 laminae fuse anteriorly = laryngeal prominence/"Adam's apple"), Cricoid (only complete ring in the whole airway, signet-ring shaped), Epiglottic (leaf-shaped, attaches to arytenoids via the aryepiglottic fold)
  • Paired: Arytenoid (pyramidal; vocal process → anchors vocal ligament; muscular process → anchors muscles), Corniculate (sits on arytenoid apex), Cuneiform (small nodule in front of corniculate)

Cavity of the larynx

  • Inlet (superior opening): directed upward/backward into laryngopharynx; wider in front than behind; bounded by epiglottis (above), inter-arytenoid fold (below), aryepiglottic folds (sides)
  • 3 internal parts: Vestibule (inlet → vestibular fold) → Sinus/ventricle (vestibular fold → vocal fold) → Infraglottic part (below vocal cords → lower border of cricoid)
  • Rima vestibuli: gap between the vestibular (false) folds
  • Rima glottidis: gap between the 2 vocal (true) folds — the narrowest part of the adult larynx (in children, the narrowest part is instead lower down, at the cricoid level — relevant for choosing pediatric airway tubes)

Vocal folds

  • False cords (vestibular folds): mucosa only, no vibration role
  • True cords (vocal folds): mobile, mucosa over the vocal ligament, avascular (so it stays pearly white and is easy to see on laryngoscopy), does the actual vibrating for voice

🔧 Mechanism: how the folds move

All intrinsic muscles act on the arytenoid cartilages to open/close or tense the rima glottidis — except cricothyroid, which is the only extrinsic-acting intrinsic muscle (tilts the thyroid cartilage to tense the cords).

  • Cricothyroid: ↑ tension of vocal cords (pitch)
  • Posterior cricoarytenoid — the only abductor — opens the rima glottidis (essential for breathing)
  • Lateral cricoarytenoid & transverse arytenoid: adduct (close) the cords
  • Oblique arytenoids + transverse arytenoid: act as a sphincter for the laryngeal inlet (protects airway during swallowing)

Vessels, nerves, lymph

  • Arteries: superior laryngeal artery (from superior thyroid) → upper half; inferior laryngeal artery (from inferior thyroid) → lower half
  • Veins: superior & inferior thyroid veins
  • Motor nerve: recurrent laryngeal nerve to all muscles except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve)
  • Sensory nerve: above the cords → internal laryngeal nerve; below the cords → recurrent laryngeal nerve; at the cords → both
  • Lymph: prelaryngeal → pretracheal/paratracheal → deep cervical nodes
✅ Quick check

Which is the only cartilage that forms a complete ring? → Cricoid. Which muscle is the only one that opens the airway? → Posterior cricoarytenoid.

🔵 PART 2 — Anatomy of the Lung

🫁 2.1 Lung — overview & shape

  • The organ where gas exchange happens; one on each side of the mediastinum (heart in between)
  • Spongy; pink in early life, dark & mottled in adults (accumulated inhaled particles)
  • Right lung 620 g, slightly heavier than left lung 570 g
  • Covered by pleura; hangs free in its own pleural cavity; attached to mediastinum only at its root

Shape — "half a cone"

  • Apex + base
  • 2 surfaces: costal (against ribs) and medial (hilum here — bronchi/vessels/lymphatics enter)
  • 3 borders: anterior & posterior (separate costal from medial surface), inferior (separates both surfaces from the base)

🔧 Apex relations — why they matter

The apex pokes above the clavicle into the root of the neck, covered by cervical pleura + suprapleural membrane. It's grooved anteriorly by the subclavian artery, and posteriorly separated from the first rib by the sympathetic trunk, superior intercostal vessels, and first thoracic nerve — this crowding is why apical lung disease can affect these neighboring structures.

⬇️ 2.2 Base & borders

  • Base: concave (molded over the diaphragm's convexity); right side is more concave because the right hemidiaphragm sits higher than the left
  • Diaphragm separates: right lung base ↔ right lobe of liver; left lung base ↔ left lobe of liver, stomach, spleen

Borders

  • Anterior border: thin & sharp; has the cardiac notch on the left lung (4th–5th intercostal spaces) — room for the heart; below the notch = the lingula (a little tongue-shaped projection)
  • Posterior border: thick & rounded, lies along the vertebral column
  • Inferior border: sharp & thin anteriorly/laterally/posteriorly; blunt medially

🔑 2.3 Root & Hilum — Right vs Left

  • Hilum: on the medial surface, where the root's structures enter/exit; lies opposite T5–T7 vertebrae
  • Root contents: main bronchus, pulmonary artery, 2 pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, broncho-pulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes, pulmonary plexuses, pleural covering (continues down as the pulmonary ligament)
  • Main bronchus: posterior-most structure; divides before entering the lung → gives an eparterial (superior lobar, above the pulmonary artery) + hyparterial (main, below the artery) branch
  • Bronchial vessels: only one bronchial artery on the right
  • Pulmonary artery: lies in front of and between the two bronchi
  • Main bronchus: one large bronchus, usually divides after entering the lung
  • Bronchial vessels: two bronchial arteries on the left
  • Pulmonary artery: lies above and anterior to the bronchus

Mediastinal surface — what's touching the hilum

Right lungLeft lung
In front: cardiac impression (pericardium, right atrium); ascending aorta area; thymusIn front: cardiac impression (pericardium, left ventricle); pulmonary trunk
Above: arch of azygos vein; SVC + right innominate vein; trachea & right vagus (behind SVC); esophagus behind tracheaAbove: arch of aorta; left common carotid/brachiocephalic vein groove; left subclavian artery groove; esophagus
Behind: esophagus (vertical groove); azygos vein (behind esophagus)Behind: descending aorta (vertical groove); esophagus
Right phrenic nerve crosses the right innominate vein, SVC, pericardial impression & IVC. Left phrenic nerve crosses the aortic arch groove & pericardial impression.
✅ Quick check

Which lung has 2 bronchial arteries? → Left. Which bronchus divides before entering the lung? → Right.

📐 2.4 Lobes & Fissures

  • Left lung: superior + inferior lobes, separated by the oblique fissure
  • Right lung: superior + middle + inferior lobes, separated by the oblique AND horizontal fissures (middle lobe is wedge-shaped, cut off from the superior lobe)
  • Oblique fissure (both lungs): starts posterior border ~6cm below apex (opp. 3rd thoracic spine) → runs along line of 6th rib → ends at inferior border at the 6th costochondral junction
  • Horizontal fissure (right lung only): starts at anterior border at the 4th costal cartilage → runs horizontally → meets the oblique fissure at the midaxillary line (6th rib)
FeatureRight lungLeft lung
Size & weightLarger & heavierSmaller & lighter
LengthShorterLonger
WidthWiderNarrower
Fissures & lobesTwo fissures, 3 lobesOne fissure, 2 lobes
Cardiac notch & lingulaNoPresent
Hilum2 bronchi, 1 bronchial artery1 bronchus, 2 bronchial arteries
Basal concavityMore concaveLess concave
SegmentsTenEight to ten

🩸 2.5 Blood supply, lymph & nerves of the lung

🔧 Mechanism: TWO separate circulations in one organ

  • Bronchial arteries = the lung's own "food delivery" — oxygenated blood for the tissue itself (trachea, bronchi down to respiratory bronchioles). 2 left bronchial arteries (from descending aorta) + 1 right (from 3rd right posterior intercostal artery or the upper left bronchial artery).
  • Pulmonary artery = the "cargo" circulation — carries de-oxygenated blood to be gas-exchanged at the alveoli (capillary plexus supplied straight from the pulmonary artery, running alongside each bronchus in an intra-segmental position).
  • So: bronchial vessels feed the pipes; the pulmonary vessels use the pipes to do their actual job (gas exchange).
  • Bronchial veins (2 per lung): right → azygos vein; left → superior hemiazygos vein
  • Pulmonary veins (2 per lung): carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium; their tributaries run between bronchopulmonary segments (intersegmental)

Lymph drainage pathway

  • Alveolar walls have no lymph vessels — lymph starts in bronchiole walls
  • Pathway: intrapulmonary nodes → bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes → tracheobronchial nodes → tracheal nodes → mediastinal nodes → broncho-mediastinal trunks → thoracic duct (left) / right lymphatic duct (right)

Nerve supply

  • Anterior & posterior pulmonary plexuses (sympathetic + parasympathetic), in front of and behind the root

🧩 2.6 Bronchopulmonary Segments

  • Each segment = supplied by its own segmental bronchus + branch of pulmonary artery + lymphatics + branch of bronchial artery
  • Pyramidal shape, apex toward the root; surrounded by connective-tissue septa (intersegmental planes, where pulmonary vein tributaries run)

🚨 Clinical mechanism

Because each segment has its own independent blood/air supply, infection usually stays confined to one segment — so surgeons can remove just the diseased segment and leave the rest of the healthy lung intact.

  • Upper lobe (3): Apical, Posterior, Anterior
  • Middle lobe (2): Lateral, Medial
  • Lower lobe (5): Apical(superior), Medial basal, Anterior basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal
  • Upper lobe (5): Apical, Posterior, Anterior, Superior lingular, Inferior lingular
  • Lower lobe (5): Apical(superior), Medial basal, Anterior basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal
  • In the left lung, apical+posterior often fuse → "Apicoposterior" segment, and the medial basal segment is often absent → so the left lung ends up with 8, 9, or 10 total segments.
🟣 PART 3 — Tutorial 1: Trachea & Bronchi

🫧 3.1 Trachea

  • Size: ~10 cm (≈4.5 inches) long, ~2.5 cm (1 inch) diameter
  • Beginning: continues from cricoid cartilage, at level of C6
  • Termination: at sternal angle / carina, opposite lower border of T4 → splits into right & left main bronchi
  • Movements: expiration → carina rises ~1 vertebra; deep inspiration → lowers to T6
  • Course: upper half in the neck midline, lower half in the thorax (superior mediastinum); deviates slightly right in its lower part

🧭 3.2 Relations of the thoracic trachea & constrictions

Arch of aorta; origins of brachiocephalic & left common carotid arteries; left innominate vein; sternum & thymus.
Esophagus; left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Right vagus nerve; right pleura & lung; arch of azygos vein.
Arch of aorta; left subclavian artery; left vagus nerve; left phrenic nerve; left pleura & lung.

Sites of normal constriction

  • Upper end — by the thyroid gland
  • Middle — by the right innominate (brachiocephalic) artery
  • Lower end — by the arch of the aorta

Vessels, nerves, lymph

  • Arteries: cervical part → inferior thyroid artery; thoracic part → right & left bronchial arteries
  • Nerves: sensory from both vagi, recurrent laryngeal nerves, and sympathetic chains
  • Lymph: para-tracheal, pre-tracheal, deep cervical nodes

↔️ 3.3 Right vs Left Bronchus

FeatureRight bronchusLeft bronchus
WidthWiderNarrower
LengthShorter (~1 in / 2.5 cm)Longer (~2 in / 5 cm)
AngleMore vertical (in line with trachea)More horizontal
Division patternDivides before entering lung → superior lobar bronchus first, then (after entering) middle + inferior lobarDivides after entering lung → superior + inferior lobar
Arch overlyingArch of azygos veinArch of aorta

🚨 Mechanism: why aspirated objects go right

Because the right bronchus is wider, shorter, and sits more vertically in line with the trachea, an inhaled foreign body "falls" the path of least resistance — straight down the right side — more often than the left.

✅ Quick check

An inhaled peanut is most likely to lodge in which bronchus, and why? → Right — wider, shorter, more vertical/in-line with the trachea.
